entry.description: Answers from a true detail in the wrong part of the passage.
entry.childHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
entry.approvalNote: Cleared on the printed review pack; returned marked up.

textProvenance.note: Ruled when written; absent from the store until now (R403/R410).
textProvenance.authority: annie-seventyeighth-return.md, read from the file, sha256 119bb12f9a3c3668677441cb8f1ab571ada1a3670dab8a19902dc28dec88cc5b

stem.text: Read lines 1 to 4. What had the Mole been doing all morning?

carriers.key: Cleaning his little home from top to bottom.

options.value: Digging out a brand new tunnel.
options.execution: Lines 9 to 13 have him scraping up a tunnel that already exists, not digging a new one, and they sit outside the window the stem names.

options.value: Cleaning his little home from top to bottom.
Painting his house blue outside and white inside.
Resting his aching back and weary arms.
Singing along with the happy birds.
options.execution: The birds sing at line 18 and the Mole never sings anywhere. A morning of work with birds outside invites it and nothing states it.

stem.text: Read lines 3 to 4. What was all over the Mole's black fur?

carriers.key: Splashes of whitewash.

options.value: Dust, which had got into his throat and eyes.
Bits of straw from his brooms.
Warm grass from the great meadow.
options.execution: The warm grass is line 15, after he comes up into the meadow — a true detail from a different part of the passage.

options.value: Splashes of whitewash.
Blue and white paint.

stem.text: Read line 8. What does 'bolted out of the house' mean here?

carriers.key: Rushed out all of a sudden.

options.value: Ate something far too fast.
Slid a bolt across to lock the door.
Climbed out slowly using a ladder.
options.execution: The ladders and steps are line 2, inside the house and before he leaves — true, and from a different part.

options.value: Rushed out all of a sudden.
Shouted 'Hang spring-cleaning!' as he went.

stem.text: In lines 11 to 14 the writer repeats words like 'scraped' and 'scrabbled'. Why does he do this?

carriers.key: To show the climb went on and on and was hard work.

options.value: To show that digging is the easiest job a mole ever does.
To show the Mole was bored and fed up with the climb.
To show the climb went on and on and was hard work.
To copy the sound of the birds singing up above.
options.execution: The birds are line 18, after he is out of the tunnel — a true sound from a different part.

options.value: To make the reader feel sorry for the Mole's sore arms.

stem.text: Read lines 14 to 15. Where did the Mole find himself when his snout came out into the sunlight?

carriers.key: Rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.

options.value: On the bank of the river.
options.execution: The bank is line 36, at the end of the river paragraph — a true place from a different part.

options.value: At the gap in the hedge.
In a boat painted blue and white.
Rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.
On a gravelled carriage-drive.

stem.text: Read lines 17 to 19. Why did the birds' singing sound almost like a shout to the Mole?

carriers.key: He had been shut underground so long that his ears were not used to it.

options.value: The birds were much louder than usual that day.
The rabbits were shouting at him from the gap.
options.execution: The rabbits shout at line 22, after this window.

options.value: The hot sun made every sound seem bigger.
He had never heard a bird sing before in his life.
He had been shut underground so long that his ears were not used to it.

stem.text: Read line 18. What does 'the carol of happy birds' mean?

carriers.key: The singing of the birds.

options.value: A Christmas song the birds had learned.
The singing of the birds.
A church bell ringing far away.
The sound of the river chattering.
options.execution: The river chatters at line 36, much later — a true sound from a different part.

options.value: A shout from someone in the meadow.

stem.text: Read lines 22 to 23. What did the elderly rabbit at the gap want from the Mole?

carriers.key: Sixpence for using the private road.

options.value: Sixpence for using the private road.
Help with his own spring-cleaning.
options.execution: Spring-cleaning is the Mole's, at lines 1 and 8. Nothing says the rabbit wants help with anything.

options.value: A ride across the river in a boat.
options.execution: The boat ride is line 63, at the far end of the passage.

options.value: To be let past the hedge himself.
Some onion sauce for his dinner.

stem.text: Read lines 24 and 25. What does 'the row' mean here?

carriers.key: The noise and fuss the Mole had made.

options.value: A line of rabbits standing together.
Moving a boat along with oars.
The noise and fuss the Mole had made.
The hedge that ran along the meadow.
options.execution: The hedge is line 21 and true, and it is a place rather than what the rabbits came out to see.

options.value: An argument between two of the rabbits.

stem.text: Read lines 29 to 33. What had the Mole never seen before in all his life?

carriers.key: A river.

options.value: A great meadow.
options.execution: The meadow is line 15 and he has just been rolling in it; a meadow being new to him is plausible and unstated.

options.value: An animal that chased and chuckled.
A face with whiskers.
options.execution: The face with whiskers is line 48, nineteen lines later.

options.value: The bright sunshine.
A river.

stem.text: The writer calls the river an animal that chases, chuckles and grips things. Read lines 29 to 33. Why does he do this?

carriers.key: To make the river seem alive, playful and always moving.

options.value: To make the river seem alive, playful and always moving.
Because a real animal was swimming in the water.
Because the river was dangerous and might grab the Mole.
Because the Water Rat lived in the bank beside it.
options.execution: The Rat's hole in the bank is line 39, after this window.

options.value: Because the Mole thought a big animal was in front of him.

stem.text: Read lines 43 to 45. What did the Mole first notice in the dark hole in the bank?

carriers.key: Something bright and small that twinkled.

options.value: A brown little face with whiskers.
Something bright and small that twinkled.
A tiny star shining in the hole.
A glow-worm.
Small neat ears and thick silky hair.
options.execution: Small neat ears and thick silky hair are line 51, at the end of the reveal.

stem.text: Lines 48 to 52 are four very short paragraphs. Each one adds one new detail. Why does the writer do this?

carriers.key: To let the reader see the face appear bit by bit, just as the Mole does.

options.value: To show that the Mole was creeping closer with every step.
To show that the Mole was afraid of the face.
To let the reader see the face appear bit by bit, just as the Mole does.
To copy the little jumps the Mole made across the meadow.
options.execution: The jumping is line 19, in the meadow, and is not what the short lines are copying.

options.value: To make the face sound as grand as it possibly could be.

stem.text: Read lines 56 to 62. The Mole says, 'Oh, it’s all very well to talk.' What does this show about him?

carriers.key: He did not know how anyone could get across the river.

options.value: He did not know how anyone could get across the river.
He thought the Water Rat was being unkind to him.
He did not want to be friends with the Water Rat.
He was too tired from his walk to move.
options.execution: The tiredness is line 35, before he ever reaches the Rat, and outside this window.

options.value: He knew all about boats but did not own one.

stem.text: Read line 65. The Mole was 'seated in the stern of a real boat'. What is the stern?

carriers.key: The back part of the boat.

options.value: A strict and serious look.
The oars that push the boat along.
options.execution: The sculls are lines 63 and 66 — true, and a different part of the boat.

options.value: A soft seat with a cushion on it.
The rope that held the boat to the bank.
The back part of the boat.

stem.text: The animals act like people, but we never forget they are animals. How does the writer do this?

carriers.key: He gives them houses, money and boats, but keeps their fur, paws and whiskers.

options.value: He keeps the animals quiet, still and dull, but lets the river chatter, gurgle and laugh.
options.execution: The animals talk all through the passage — the rabbit at line 22, the Rat and Mole at lines 54 to 57 and 64 — so the claim is false of the text. The chattering, gurgling and laughing river at lines 30 and 36 is the true detail it borrows.

options.value: He gives them human names, and leaves the animal ones behind.
He tells the reader, plainly and often, that these animals are really people.
He gives them houses, money and boats, but keeps their fur, paws and whiskers.
He makes every animal speak, move and think in exactly the same way.

stem.text: The Bennet daughters did not meet Mr Bingley when he called at their house. Read lines 5 to 8. What were they able to find out about him?

carriers.key: What colour his coat was, and what colour his horse was.

options.value: That he was cheerful and talked to everybody.
options.execution: Being cheerful and talking to everybody is Mr Bingley at lines 36 and 37, at the ball — true, and a different part of the passage. In the window, line 8 answers the stem: 'window, that he wore a blue coat and rode'.

options.value: That he had ten thousand pounds a year.
What colour his coat was, and what colour his horse was.
That he stayed about ten minutes with their father.
That he liked the big house he had taken.

stem.text: Mr Bingley hoped for something on this visit that he did not get. Read lines 5 to 6. What was it?

carriers.key: A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.

options.value: A book from Mr Bennet's library.
A look at Mr Bennet's daughters.
A chance to invite the Bennets to dinner at his own house.
A ride on Mr Bennet's black horse.
A dance with the eldest Miss Bennet.
options.execution: The dancing is lines 36 to 41, at the assembly, weeks after this visit. In the window, line 5 answers the stem: 'him in his library. He had entertained hopes of'.

stem.text: Mr Bingley said no to the Bennets' dinner. Read lines 9 to 12. What reason did his answer give?

carriers.key: He had to be in London the next day.

options.value: He had promised to dine with Lady Lucas instead.
He did not want to meet the Bennet daughters.
He was busy planning the courses for a dinner of his own.
He had to be in London the next day.
He had gone to London to gather a big group for the ball.
options.execution: The London party is Lady Lucas's guess at lines 15 to 17, after the refusal and not part of it. In the window, line 11 answers the stem: 'which deferred it all. Mr. Bingley was obliged to'.

stem.text: Mr Bingley's answer upset Mrs Bennet. Read lines 13 to 16. What was she most afraid of?

carriers.key: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.

options.value: That he would keep moving about and never really live at Netherfield.
That her dinner had all been cooked and would now be wasted.
That he had gone to London to look for guests for the ball.
That the girls would have to meet twelve strange ladies.
options.execution: The twelve ladies are line 18, and it is the GIRLS who grieve over them at line 18, not Mrs Bennet. In the window, line 14 answers the stem: 'his arrival in Hertfordshire; and she began to fear'.

options.value: That Mr Bingley did not like her daughters.

stem.text: Read lines 17 to 21. Line 21 says: 'when the party entered the assembly-room'. What does 'party' mean here?

carriers.key: A group of people who arrive together.

options.value: A celebration with food, music and games.
The ball that Mr Bingley talked of giving at Netherfield.
options.execution: The Netherfield ball is line 38, at the very end of the evening — a true event from a different part. In the window, line 21 answers the stem: 'cousin. And when the party entered the assembly-room, it'.

options.value: A group of people who arrive together.
A group of people who run a country together.
Everybody who came to the assembly that night.

stem.text: When Mr Darcy first walked in, the room thought very well of him. Read lines 26 to 30. Why?

carriers.key: Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.

options.value: Because he danced with lots of different ladies.
Because he spoke kindly to everyone he was introduced to.
Because he was the tallest man in the room.
Because of his looks, and because of the news that he was very rich.
Because he owned a large estate in Derbyshire.
options.execution: The Derbyshire estate is line 33, and it appears only when the room has turned against him. In the window, line 27 answers the stem: 'drew the attention of the room by his fine'.

stem.text: Read lines 41 to 43. The writer says: 'His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in the world.' What do these short, sure sentences do?

carriers.key: They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.

options.value: They prove that Mr Darcy really was the worst man alive.
They show that the writer had run out of things to say about him.
They make the room's quick opinion sound like a settled fact.
They show that Mr Darcy had at last made up his mind about something.
They tell us that Mr Darcy said nothing to anybody all evening.
options.execution: Line 41 has him 'speaking occasionally to one of his own party', so he does speak.

stem.text: Mrs Bennet disliked Mr Darcy more strongly than anybody else in the room did. Read lines 44 to 46. What made her feeling so strong?

carriers.key: He had been rude about one of her daughters.

options.value: He had been rude about one of her daughters.
He would not let anyone introduce him to her.
options.execution: Declining to be introduced is line 40, and it is to any other LADY, not to Mrs Bennet in particular. In the window, line 44 answers the stem: 'Amongst the most violent against him was Mrs. Bennet'.

options.value: He had told Mr Bennet that he did not like the neighbourhood.
Mr Bingley had chosen to dance with her eldest daughter.
He was the proudest man in the world, and she hated proud people.

stem.text: Elizabeth had to sit down for two dances. Read lines 47 to 48. Why?

carriers.key: There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.

options.value: She did not feel like dancing that evening.
Mr Darcy had refused to dance with her.
She wanted to listen to Mr Darcy and Mr Bingley talking.
There were not enough gentlemen for all the ladies.
Her eldest sister was dancing with Mr Bingley.
options.execution: Her eldest sister dancing with Mr Bingley is line 60, true, and not the reason line 47 gives.

stem.text: Read lines 51 and 52. Mr Bingley says to his friend: 'I hate to see you standing about by yourself in this stupid manner.' What is Mr Bingley trying to do?

carriers.key: Get his friend to join the dancing.

options.value: Tell his friend off for being rude about the ladies.
options.execution: The rudeness about the ladies is lines 55 and 56, in Mr Darcy's reply, after this speech. In the window, line 51 answers the stem: '“Come, Darcy,” said he, “I must have you dance'.

options.value: Get his friend to join the dancing.
Ask his friend to leave the ball and go home.
Make his friend feel sorry for the ladies who have no partner.

stem.text: At the end, Elizabeth turns what happened into a story for her friends. Read lines 70 to 73. What does this tell us about her?

carriers.key: She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.

options.value: She has completely forgiven Mr Darcy.
She can find the funny side of things, even when she has been treated badly.
She wants her friends to feel sorry for her.
What Mr Darcy said did not bother her at all.
She thinks Mr Darcy is a fine, handsome man.
options.execution: The praise of his looks is line 30, from the ladies of the room, and it is withdrawn by line 34. In the window, line 70 answers the stem: 'Mr. Bingley followed his advice. Mr. Darcy walked off'.

stem.text: What did Matthew do when he first saw the girl? (lines 4 to 6)

carriers.key: He slipped past her without looking at her.

options.value: He slipped past her without looking at her.
He noticed her red hair and freckled face.
options.execution: True of the description at lines 37 and 38, but line 6 says he did not look at her.

options.value: He asked her who she was waiting for.
He slipped past her, glancing at her as he went.

stem.text: In lines 20 to 22, what does the stationmaster say Mrs Spencer did at the station?

carriers.key: She came off the train with the girl and left her with him.

options.value: She came off the train with the girl and left her with him.
She waited beside the girl until Matthew came.
She was to bring a boy over from Nova Scotia.
options.execution: True of the passage, but from line 18 and spoken by Matthew, not by the stationmaster here. In the window, line 20 answers the stem: '“Guess there’s some mistake,” he said. “Mrs. Spencer came'.

options.value: She took the girl into her charge from him.

stem.text: What does the girl do once she decides Matthew is coming to her? (lines 47 to 49)

carriers.key: She stands up, takes her bag and holds out her hand.

options.value: She stands up, takes her bag and holds out her hand.
She stays sitting and watches him come closer.
options.execution: True of line 33, before she stands; the question asks what she does next. In the window, line 47 answers the stem: 'Matthew, however, was spared the ordeal of speaking first'.

options.value: She stands up and holds out both her hands.
She walks along the platform to meet him.

stem.text: What does Matthew ask the girl to do at the end? (lines 64 and 65)

carriers.key: Come along with him, and hand him her bag.

options.value: Go and sit in the ladies' waiting room.
options.execution: True of line 14, where the stationmaster asks it; Matthew never does. In the window, line 64 answers the stem: '“I’m sorry I was late,” he said shyly. “Come'.

options.value: Come along with him, and carry her own bag.
Tell him her name before they set off.
Come along with him, and hand him her bag.

stem.text: What came down across the road in front of them? (lines 22 to 24)

carriers.key: An oak tree, torn up by the roots.

options.value: An oak tree, torn up by the roots.
A great branch from one of the swaying trees.
Part of the wooden bridge, carried off by the flood.
A shower of dry leaves blown across the road.
options.execution: True of line 4, at the start of the journey, not here. In the window, line 22 answers the stem: 'The words were scarcely out of his mouth when'.

stem.text: What happens when Uncle Podger first lifts up the picture? (lines 18 and 19)

carriers.key: He drops it, the frame comes off, and he cuts himself.

options.value: He hangs it crooked and has to start again.
He drops the hammer on somebody's toes.
options.execution: True of line 48, but that is much later, at the first blow. In the window, line 18 answers the stem: 'And then he would lift up the picture, and'.

options.value: He drops it and the glass stays whole.
He drops it, the frame comes off, and he cuts himself.

stem.text: Read lines 38 and 39. On line 38 Uncle Podger takes 'the rule' and re-measures. What is a 'rule' here?

carriers.key: A tool for measuring length.

options.value: A law about how the job has to be done.
A line drawn on the wall to work from.
options.execution: Reuses the mark on the wall from line 34; the rule is a separate thing he takes up. In the window, line 38 answers the stem: 'down. And he would take the rule, and re-measure'.

options.value: A habit he always follows when working.
A tool for measuring length.

stem.text: What does Uncle Podger fall onto when the string slips? (lines 43 to 45)

carriers.key: The piano.

options.value: The piano.
The kitchen-chair he had been standing on.
The charwoman's corns.
Somebody's toes, with a yell.
options.execution: True of line 48, but that is the hammer falling, not Uncle Podger. In the window, line 43 answers the stem: 'inches beyond what was possible for him to reach'.

stem.text: The writer says 'would' again and again. He would shout, he would drop it, he would call us fools. What does that tell us about this day?

carriers.key: It is not one day at all, but what happened every single time.

options.value: It is not one clear memory, but a guess at what may have happened.
It tells us the picture was never hung, though he says it was.
It tells us the story is remembered years after it all happened.
options.execution: True of line 1, which is about remembering, not about how often it happened.

options.value: It is not one day at all, but what happened every single time.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 3. How does Roberta wake Phyllis?

carriers.key: By pulling her hair, gently but hard enough.

options.value: By pulling her hair, gently but hard enough.
By shouting at her to wake up.
options.execution: Roberta does shout, at line 4, and that is after Phyllis has begun to stir. In the window, line 1 answers the stem: 'Next morning Roberta woke Phyllis by pulling her hair'.

options.value: By pulling the blankets off her bed.
Phyllis wakes Roberta by pulling her hair.

stem.text: Read lines 8 to 10. Which of these is true about the girls' washing?

carriers.key: One of them works the pump while the other washes.

options.value: They wash in their own bedroom.
They wash in a basin.
options.execution: Basin washing is real in the passage, but at line 11, as the thing compared. In the window, line 9 answers the stem: 'when they got down they washed as much as'.

options.value: One of them works the pump while the other washes.
The splashing spoiled it for them.

stem.text: Read lines 20 to 23. What do the children use for the table?

carriers.key: A glass ash-tray for salt, and a baking-tin for bread.

options.value: A glass ash-tray for salt, and a baking-tin for bread.
A baking-tin for salt, and a glass ash-tray for bread.
They find all the right things and lay them out.
Bread and butter, set out ready on the table.
options.execution: That table is at line 51, in the forgotten room, and line 23 says they had no bread.

stem.text: Look at lines 48 and 49. What does 'agitation' on line 48 mean there?

carriers.key: being worried and in a hurry

options.value: the stirring or shaking of a liquid
the half darkness of the house that night
being worried and in a hurry
the excitement of finding a forgotten room
options.execution: That happens at line 46, the morning after, and this word is about the night before. In the window, line 48 answers the stem: 'The forgotten room opened out of the kitchen. In'.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 3. Why does the bus stop at the caravan park?

carriers.key: Because there is nowhere for it to turn round.

options.value: Because there is nowhere for it to turn round.
Because that is as far as he had ever got before.
options.execution: True of him at line 5, and it is not why the bus turns back.

options.value: Because nobody lives any further out than that.
Because the two miles of sea wall begin there.

stem.text: Read lines 18 to 23. What lies in the mud below the wall?

carriers.key: A boat with its ribs showing, and a gull on it.

options.value: A boat with its ribs showing, and a gull on it.
A half mile of black posts leaning into the channel.
What is left of an old bridge across the channel.
The remains of a row of four cottages.
options.execution: The cottages are real, at line 7, and they are out at Saltmere, not here.

stem.text: Read lines 21 to 23. What does Mrs Otis take the stain to be?

carriers.key: Something that has been spilt on the floor.

options.value: Something she was quite unconscious of.
The blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, murdered there.
options.execution: True, but at line 28, and line 22 says she does not yet know what it means.

options.value: A shadow the firelight was throwing on the boards.
Something that has been spilt on the floor.

stem.text: Read lines 24 to 27. What does Mrs Otis's reply show about her?

carriers.key: She wants the mark gone rather than the story explained.

options.value: She wants the mark gone rather than the story explained.
She is frightened by what the old housekeeper has just told her.
She rather likes a blood-stain in a sitting-room.
She doubts the story rather than the stain itself.
options.execution: True at line 55, where the Otises are said to be 'not afraid of ghosts' — that is the family's scepticism about the STORY, and it sits fifty lines past this window. Inside the window, lines 26 and 27 answer the stem: Mrs Otis says 'I don't at all care for blood-stains in a sitting-room. It must be removed at once' — she addresses the mess and never the tale.

stem.text: Look at lines 6 to 9. What did Jim find inside the barrel?

carriers.key: There was hardly an apple left in it.

options.value: A heavy man sat down close by it.
There was hardly an apple left in it.
There was straw packed round the apples.
The moon was shining white on the sail.
options.execution: True at line 59, far outside this window; lines 6 to 9 are in the dark.

stem.text: Look at lines 18 to 26 and 43 to 49. How do Silver's two speeches differ?

carriers.key: First he talks of his own money, then of using other men.

options.value: First he talks of his own money, then of using other men.
First he says the life is rough, then he says the pay is good.
First he calls Dick square, then he trusts him with the keg.
options.execution: True at line 37 and at line 56, both outside the two windows named here. In the window, line 22 answers the stem: 'it all away, some here, some there, and none'.

options.value: First he spends all he earns, then he puts a little away.

stem.text: Look at lines 4 to 7 and 60 to 67. What has changed between the two heaps of goods?

carriers.key: His pockets hold the same sort of trash, but he paid nothing for it.

options.value: He had bits of toys and marbles, and by the end he has twelve marbles.
His pockets hold the same sort of trash, but he paid nothing for it.
He grew rich first, but then he gave up buying the boys.
His next turn went to Billy Fisher, and a kite came back for it.
options.execution: True at line 58, outside both windows; lines 4 to 7 and 60 to 67 never name Billy.

stem.text: Look at lines 15 to 19. What did Tom want that he did not take?

carriers.key: The apple that Ben was eating.

options.value: A good look at the steamboat.
The gentle sweep he gave his brush.
A turn at swimming with the other boys.
options.execution: True at line 23, outside this window; lines 15 to 19 never mention swimming.

options.value: The apple that Ben was eating.

stem.text: Look at lines 28 to 31 and 60 to 66. What does the second noise do that the first does not?

carriers.key: The first noise he leaves behind, and the second one follows him.

options.value: The first is like thunder, and the second is like a dragged chain.
The first noise he leaves behind, and the second one follows him.
The bells ring first, and the door bangs a long while after.
The flame leaps up first, and then it falls again in the grate.
options.execution: True at line 69 and line 70, outside both windows; neither window has a flame in it. In the window, line 30 answers the stem: 'own. Scrooge was not a man to be frightened'.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 4. What does Dr Mortimer point out of the window?

carriers.key: The first sight of the moor itself.

options.value: The first sight of the moor itself.
The green squares of the fields.
The small station where they get down.
options.execution: True at line 11, outside this window; lines 1 to 4 have them still on the train.

options.value: The road that runs up to the Hall.

stem.text: Look at lines 5 to 10 and 45 to 46. What has changed in Sir Henry?

carriers.key: He is a brave comrade at first, but the moor has silenced him.

options.value: His eyes were fixed upon it, and his face was eager to see it.
He is a brave comrade at first, but the moor has silenced him.
He falls silent first, but Watson had judged him brave.
He talks of electric lamps, and then he says nothing more.
options.execution: True at line 69 and line 71, outside both windows; neither window has him speak. In the window, line 9 answers the stem: 'lie before us, this was at least a comrade'.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 5. What did Captain Brown bring up at the party?

carriers.key: Some numbers of a book coming out in parts.

options.value: Some numbers of a book coming out in parts.
Conversation, and comparing of cards, and tricks.
The scene about a party given at Bath.
options.execution: True at line 23, outside this window; that comes later in the evening. In the window, line 1 answers the stem: 'When the trays re-appeared with biscuits and wine, punctually'.

options.value: A newspaper he had brought in with him.

stem.text: Look at lines 38 to 42. What does Miss Jenkyns recommend to Boz?

carriers.key: That he take Dr Johnson's style as a model.

options.value: That he take Dr Johnson's style as a model.
That her father take Boz for a model.
That he form his own style upon her letters.
That he stop publishing his work in numbers.
options.execution: True at line 35, outside this window; lines 38 to 42 say nothing about numbers.

stem.text: Look at lines 50 and 51. Why will the narrator not vouch for what she reports?

carriers.key: She only has it at second hand from others.
